lead: A protection domain groups a set of subjects, a set of objects, and the access rights that subjects may exercise on those objects. It lets the operating system decide quickly whether a request is allowed. The idea is used in all modern OSes to keep user programs separate and to protect files, devices and memory.
prereq: You need: Goals and principles of protection and basic OS concepts from Unit 1.

blocks.text: A protection domain is a logical container. It contains subjects, objects and the rights that link them. A subject is an active entity such as a process or a user. An object is a passive entity such as a file, a device or a memory segment. An access right is a verb like read, write or execute.

items: Subject – a running program or a user identity.
Object – a resource that can be protected.
Right – the operation that a subject may perform on an object.

blocks.text: Some syllabi call the same idea a security domain. Only a few universities teach the domain model in depth, so the description stays concise.
The domain is enforced by a reference monitor. The monitor is a trusted component that mediates every request.

items: Subject sends a request to the reference monitor.
Monitor looks up the subject’s rights in the domain.
If the right matches, the monitor permits the access.
Otherwise the monitor denies the request.

blocks.text: The reference monitor must be complete, tamper‑proof and verifiable. Completeness means no request can bypass it. Tamper‑proofness means the monitor cannot be altered by a subject. Verifiable means the monitor is small enough to be examined formally, ensuring its correctness. (Being always invoked follows from completeness.)

items: All subjects are identified before the request reaches the monitor.
The monitor checks the domain’s access‑right table.
The decision is made before the object is touched.

blocks.text: In practice the monitor is implemented as part of the kernel. It uses data structures such as the access matrix (see Access matrix) but the matrix itself is not the domain.

spec.aria: Shows a subject asking the reference monitor for access to an object.

examples.question: Process P1 (subject) wants to read file F1 (object). The protection domain contains the following rights: P1 – read → F1, P2 – write → F1, P1 – execute → progX. Is the request allowed?
steps: Identify the subject (P1) and the object (F1).
Look up the rights of P1 in the domain.
P1 has a read right on F1.
The requested operation is read, which matches the stored right.
Therefore the reference monitor permits the access.

traps: Confusing a protection domain with the access‑matrix table – the domain is the logical grouping, the matrix is one way to store rights.
Assuming the reference monitor can be bypassed by a privileged user – completeness forbids any bypass.
Mixing up subject and object order in the rights list – the right always reads subject → operation → object.

quiz.q: What three components make up a protection domain?
Why must a reference monitor be tamper‑proof?
quiz.a: If a subject could modify the monitor, it could grant itself illegal rights, breaking security.

quiz.q: Given a domain where user U2 has write access to file D2, is a request by U2 to delete D2 allowed?
quiz.a: Delete is not the same as write; the request is denied. Note: In most file systems, delete requires write permission on the containing directory, not on the file itself. Since only write on D2 is given, the delete request is denied.

quiz.q: A system logs a request that was denied by the reference monitor. Explain how you would verify whether the denial was correct using the domain definition.
quiz.a: Identify the subject, object and operation; look up the subject’s rights in the domain; if the right is absent, the denial is correct.

quiz.q: What property ensures that every access request passes through the reference monitor?
If a new process P3 is created, what steps must the OS take to place it in a protection domain?
quiz.a: Assign P3 a subject identifier, decide which protection domain it belongs to (e.g., the user’s domain), add it to that domain, and initialise its default rights entry in the access‑right table.

beyond: Not for the exam. In industry, protection domains are used to implement containers and micro‑VMs that isolate workloads. Research explores fine‑grained domains for IoT devices where memory and power are limited. Emerging curricula add domain‑based policies to cloud‑native security courses. Look for papers on “reference monitor enforcement in hardware” and “capability vs. domain models”.
